newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Bank of Canada cuts rates to lowest in decades.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bank of Canada cuts rates to lowest in decades.

text.p: The Bank of Canada cut interest rates on Friday to their lowest levels in decades, with analysts speculating that rates may fall even more before the year is through.
The central bank cut its key bank rate by 25 basis points to 3.25 percent, bringing the rate to its lowest point since December 1961. The bank rate is similar to the U.S. Federal funds rate.

Canada's major chartered banks quickly responded by lowering their prime lending rates to 4.75 percent, the lowest since March 1956. A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. Financial markets were steady after the cut.
It was the 11th cut this year by the Bank of Canada and the 10th independent of the U.S. Federal Reserve. The Bank of Canada has now cut rates by 500 basis points since May 1995.

The widely expected rate cut was prompted by recent strength in the Canadian dollar and evidence that past easing was having little impact on economic growth. Analysts refused to rule out the possibility the Bank of Canada would cut rates even further this year.
"It's very dangerous to stand in front of the Bank of Canada's easing train," said Andrew Spence, senior economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Toronto.
Analysts said the central bank will likely cut rates again if the currency keeps strengthening and economic indicators remain weak.

"The data we've seen lately has been sluggish," said Michael Gregory, a Toronto-based economist with Lehman Brothers. "With the Fed on hold, they (Bank of Canada) have an opportunity to continue to ratchet rates lower until we get some signs of life in the economy."

The rate cut followed a government report that showed Canada's unemployment rate rose to 10 percent in October from 9.9 percent in September. Economists had forecast the rate would drop to 9.7 percent.
"The numbers don't mean it's jobless growth. The numbers tell us that growth has been too slow," said Canadian Industry Minister John Manley after the report.
Another report showed that housing starts fell unexpectedly by 9.8 percent in October.

The Bank of Canada said in a news release that the cut was designed to offset the impact of a stronger dollar on monetary conditions in Canada. The Canadian dollar strengthened past C$1.3333 (US$0.75) this week to its highest point in more than a year.
The central bank sees a stronger currency as having the same impact on the economy as an interest rate hike because it makes exports less competitive.
Dealers said the strength of the currency for the rest of the year will be the key factor in whether the latest reduction marks the end of the easing cycle.

"One has to wonder at what point does the bank decide it no longer needs to offset that future appreciation in the exchange rate. I think we're getting very close to that point," said Deutsche's Spence.
